title: Roads of Destiny…
reviewNotes: Montages, captions and complete native diagrams reviewed. Final mating patterns only, after Black has accepted the queen on h5 or b5. Both complete fourteen-piece diagrams are visually reconstructed: native32 confirms Kxh5 at94 seconds; native51/52 confirm Kxb5 at143–146 seconds. The right pattern has White Ka7/Nd5/a3/b3/h3 against Kh5/Qe8/Nd7/Ng5/a5/c4/h4/h6/h7. The left has White Ka7/Nf5/a3/b3/h3 against Kb5/Qe8/Nc5/Nf7/Bf3/a5/h4/h6/h7. The branches teach Nf4# and Nd4# respectively, with exact finite certificates ending in actual mate. The queen offers themselves, refusals such as Kg7 or Kf5, the skewer conversion and the original seventeen-piece root remain outside this proof. These two mate-in-one exercises must not be read as certification that Black had to accept either queen offer.
transcript: Roads of Destiny, that's the name of the chess position in front of you. A position composed of a hundred years ago and yet so beautiful that it deserved its own name. You see, black is up a bishop and a few pawns, but it is white to move and so it's up to white to decide what's next. And indeed white starts with queen to c3, a very precise check that forces the black king to make a choice. We can easily exclude a few options. For example, king to e4 would allow a skewer of the king and queen winning the queen and the game. And if the king goes up like this, there is going to be a knight fork, again picking up the queen and winning the game for white. And none of these squares are available. So, the black king has to take one of the two knights. Taking the knight on the right would not be wise because this drops the bishop with check and forces the king to make yet another choice, either to go back and get forked like this or to go to one of these two squares. Now, this would not be wise. This is simply a checkmate in one move like this. But if the [music] king goes to g6, this is where we start to see some brilliant ideas unfolding. White plays queen to g4 anyway and this time black has the option to cover the checkmate threat with knight to g5. And now it might seem like black is simply out of the woods. It still has an extra knight and a bunch of pawns and there is no checkmate. But white has the brilliant and beautiful queen to h5, sacrificing the queen completely, skewering the king and queen so that if the king moves, we're going to win the queen. But if the king takes, this would be a checkmate with the knight. So, black cannot allow this and going all the way back to when it decided to take this knight, black realizes that it has to take the knight on d5. Taking this pawn would be unwise. After king to e5, there's no follow up. So, white continues with his secret plan and goes queen to d4 check, Now pushing the king further to c6, and only now takes the pawn. And you might notice that there are some similarities with the other situation. The king cannot go anywhere. It has to block with a knight. And this time, there are no tricks with the queen. Except that there are. Queen to b5, same exact pattern. We sacrifice the queen for the skewer. And incredibly, after the king [music] takes, we still have a knight checkmate like this. If you love incredible chess, follow for more.
